title: Die Slang-Ampel: grün, gelb, rot
summary: Real spoken German by traffic light — what you can say to anyone, what stays among friends, and what to recognise but never deploy

blocks.title: Grün: sag es überall
blocks.body: Everyday German is full of colour, but not all of it fits every room. Think of a **traffic light**. **Green** words are friendly and safe *everywhere* — with your boss, at the Amt, with your landlord. Learn these first and use them freely.
blocks.callout: *Alles klar?* — *Alles klar.* is the most useful two-line exchange in German. It means both „got it?” and „all good.”

blocks.title: Tap to hear the green tier
Gelb: nur unter Freunden
blocks.body: **Yellow** words are casual — fine with friends, wrong with your boss or a stranger. The famous trap is **geil**: it means „awesome,” but it *literally* means „horny.” Great among mates, a disaster in a job interview. Same with **Alter** (dude) and **Bock haben** (to be up for something).
blocks.callout: Golden rule: if you'd hesitate to say the English version to your boss, keep the German one for friends.

blocks.prompt: You're telling your boss the project turned out great. Which word do you NOT use?
blocks.explain: *geil* is yellow — friends only, because it literally means „horny.” With a boss, say *super* or *top*.

blocks.title: Grün oder gelb? Gleiche Idee, anderer Raum

pairs.note: Same enthusiasm, very different register. *geil* literally means „horny” — never with the boss.
*Bock haben* = to be in the mood for. Warm with mates, off-key at the Amt.

blocks.title: Rot: erkennen, nicht benutzen
blocks.body: **Red** words you should *recognise* — you'll hear them — but not reach for. Interesting quirk: German cursing skews **scatological and religious** (*Mist, Scheiße, verdammt, Herrgott*), not disease-based like some languages. **Scheiße** is mild but audible in public; stronger stuff (*verpiss dich, Arschloch*) is genuinely rude. We flag these so you understand them, not so you use them.
blocks.callout: Recognising a swear ≠ needing to say it. Understanding the room is the real skill.

blocks.prompt: Your friend claims something absurd. React with the one-word German for „Nonsense!”.
blocks.explain: *Quatsch!* — green, friendly, everywhere. It's the good-natured „no way / that's rubbish.”

blocks.prompt: Jonas texts: „Hast du Bock, heute in die Kneipe zu gehen?” What's he asking?
options: Are you up for going to the pub today?
Are you angry about the pub?
blocks.explain: *Bock haben* = to be up for / in the mood for. (*Bock* literally means „billy goat,” but the idiom has nothing to do with goats.)

blocks.scene: Jonas texts you to come out — full casual mode, yellow tier everywhere.

lines.speaker: Jonas
lines.target: Ey, na? Hast du Bock, heute Abend in die Kneipe zu gehen?
lines.en: Hey, so? You up for the pub tonight?
lines.spotlight: *Bock haben* + *ey* — pure yellow tier. Perfect with a friend, never with a stranger.

lines.speaker: You
lines.target: Klar. Aber ich bin echt müde, nur ein Bier.
lines.en: Sure. But I'm really tired, just one beer.

lines.speaker: Jonas
lines.target: Quatsch, ein Bier kann jeder. Komm schon!
lines.en: Nonsense, anyone can do one beer. Come on!

lines.speaker: Jonas
lines.target: Na ja, dafür wird's geil. Die Band von gestern spielt wieder — voll krass.
lines.en: Well, but it'll be awesome for it. Yesterday's band is playing again — totally wild.
lines.spotlight: *geil* and *krass* — friends-only words. Fine here, off-limits with the boss.

lines.speaker: You
lines.target: Alles klar, überredet. Feierabend heißt Feierabend.
lines.en: All right, you win. Off-hours are off-hours.

blocks.prompt: Which three „green” words do you want to start using this week? And which „yellow” word have you already heard in the wild? Write one sentence for each — and note who you'd say it to.
starters: Zu meinem Chef sage ich lieber…
